## At a glance

**Guiding question:** How does a team protect findings data, the model version and availability?\
**For:** clinical IT, research software engineers, data stewards, and the clinical leads who decide whether a tool
stays on; the core reading needs no programming. · **Prerequisites:** a reproducible R project from @sec-b04; monitoring
and restart in @sec-b20; the data flow in @sec-b23.\
**In the course:** [W7 · Regulation, data protection and
incident](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w7-regulation-data-protection-incident.html)
(control matrix and table-top exercise), [W8 · Colloquium and
decision](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w8-colloquium-and-decision.html) ·
**Data:** synthetic (model file, logs and test cases generated in the chapter) · **Core reading time:** about 11
minutes
:::

## Case and decision {#sec-b24-case}

Monday, 07:40, in the fictitious emergency department of @sec-b09. The service provider of the fracture alert reports
that one of its support logs contains part of a radiology report. Ten minutes later, the routine release check on the
inference server shows that the installed model file does not have the checksum of the approved release. The
consultant in charge has to decide whether the alert stays on. She switches it off. All radiographs now go through the
regular reporting pathway, as on any day without the tool, so no patient waits longer for a report. The IT security
officer blocks the provider's remote access, secures the logs and starts a restore from a verified copy. The alert will
come back only after a synthetic test case has passed and the system owner has signed. The night shift works without
the second look; nobody works without a report.

## Core reading {#sec-b24-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · recommended reading for W7 (table-top material) · about 11 minutes · ends before ‘Lab’
:::

**A threat model in four questions.** What are we protecting (assets)? Where can it be attacked (attack surface)?
Where does trust change (trust boundaries)? Who is responsible for each part (owners)? @fig-b24-threat answers these
questions for the fictional second-look service. Radiographs go from the imaging device to the image archive, the
inference server reads them, applies the model and writes a marker back to the reporting worklist. The model arrives
from the provider's release repository; the provider's support team can connect remotely; logs go to a log store;
backups go to a separate store. Five points of the attack surface are numbered. Only one of them – the remote support
access – is visible to clinicians, and the incident in the case used two of them.


::: {.cell}

**Each control needs a test.** @tbl-b24-controls assigns a control, an observable test and an owner to each asset.
**The key assumption of this chapter: a control counts only if a test shows that it works, with the expected result
written down before the test is run.** A policy that says "access is restricted" is not a control until someone has
tried a forbidden access and seen it refused.

| Asset | Goal | Control | Observable test (expected result) | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Images and reports | Confidentiality | Least privilege: each role reads only what its task needs; provider support has no read access to report text; deny by default | Support role requests a report: refused, refusal logged without content | System owner, IT security |
| Model file and configuration | Integrity | Release record with SHA-256 checksum from the provider's release process; server refuses to load a file whose checksum differs | Load a modified file: refused | Provider (release), clinical IT (installation) |
| Alert and reporting | Availability | Regular reporting pathway as fallback; backups with checksums; restore procedure | Restore from a verified copy; synthetic test cases give the expected outputs | System owner, radiology lead |
| Logs | Integrity, minimal content | Event logs without health data; entries chained by hashes | Edit one entry: chain check fails at that entry; scan finds no forbidden fields | IT security, data protection officer |
| Keys | Confidentiality | Encryption at rest and in transit; keys in a separate key store with named custodians and rotation | Restore succeeds only with the key from the key store; key rotation rehearsed | IT security |

: Controls, tests and owners for the fictional second-look service. Fictional roles; the tests of the first four rows are demonstrated in the lab with synthetic data. {#tbl-b24-controls}

**Where the duties come from.** The [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj/eng) requires security appropriate to the risk, including the ability to ensure the
ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of systems, the ability to restore availability and
access to personal data in a timely manner after an incident, and a process for regularly testing the effectiveness
of the measures (Art. 32(1)(b)–(d)) [@eu2016dsgvo; Law]. For medical device software, the [MDR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/745/oj/eng) requires development
according to the state of the art including information security, and minimum IT security requirements set by the
manufacturer, including protection against unauthorised access (Annex I, Sections 17.2 and 17.4) [@eu2017mdr; Law].
High-risk AI systems must allow automatic logging, and deployers must keep the logs under their control for at least
six months unless other law provides otherwise ([AI Act](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng) Art. 12 and 26(6)); for devices these duties apply from
2 August 2028 [@eu2024aiact; @eu2026omnibus; Law]. The German Federal Office for Information Security (Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der
Informationstechnik, BSI) recommends protecting the integrity of trained models with cryptographic measures and
suitable monitoring and logging (measure M5) [@bsi2024genki; Guidance]. NIST describes the AI supply chain as an attack
surface and names the basic check: the provider publishes cryptographic hashes, and the recipient verifies them; models
should be treated as untrusted system components [@nist2025ai1002, Sec. 3.2; Guidance]. The same idea appears in
NIST's secure development framework as a mechanism for verifying software release integrity, for example by posting
hashes or signing code (practice PS.2) [@souppaya2022ssdf; Guidance].

**Checksum and signature.** A checksum such as SHA-256 is a fingerprint of a file: if a single byte changes, the
fingerprint changes. It shows that the installed file is the approved one only if the expected value comes from a
trustworthy source, such as a signed release record. A digital signature binds that value to the key of whoever
released it. The lab demonstrates the checksum part; signature verification uses separate tools and key management
and is described here only conceptually.

**Log events, not content.** The incident began because a debugging setting wrote complete requests, including
report text, into a support log that left the hospital. A useful log records that something happened, not what the
patient has: time, a random request number, the model version's checksum, whether an alert was shown, the duration
and an error code. The link between request number and examination stays inside the image archive. Logs can be made
tamper-evident by chaining: each entry contains the hash of the previous one, so that a deleted or edited entry breaks
the chain.

**Recovery is a test, not a promise.** NIST's contingency planning guide puts it briefly: testing validates recovery
capabilities [@swanson2010contingency, Executive Summary; Guidance]. A restore that has never been tried is an
assumption. A recovery test uses synthetic cases with known expected outputs, so that it can be run at any time
without touching patient data.

**Question for the workshop:** The nightly backup ran at 02:00 on Monday, after the wrong model file was installed on
Sunday. What does your restore procedure do with that backup, and who decides which older copy is used?

## Lab {#sec-b24-lab}

The lab demonstrates the three control tests with synthetic objects only. Nothing is written to disk and nothing
connects to a network; in practice the same functions work on files (`digest(file = ...)`).

**Test 1 – an unauthorised read is refused and logged without content.**


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Role-based permissions: TRUE = may read (deny by default for everything not listed)
permissions <- data.frame(
  role           = c("radiologist", "ed_clinician", "inference_service", "vendor_support", "it_admin"),
  image_pixels   = c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE),
  report_text    = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE),
  model_file     = c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE),
  service_events = c(FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)
)
allowed_log_fields <- c("time", "request_id", "role", "resource", "decision")

request_access <- function(role, resource, time, log) {
  granted <- role %in% permissions$role && resource %in% names(permissions)[-1] &&
    isTRUE(permissions[permissions$role == role, resource])
  entry <- data.frame(time = time, request_id = sprintf("R%04d", nrow(log) + 1), role = role,
                      resource = resource, decision = if (granted) "granted" else "refused")
  list(granted = granted, log = rbind(log, entry))
}

log <- data.frame(time = character(), request_id = character(), role = character(),
                  resource = character(), decision = character())
r1 <- request_access("vendor_support", "report_text", "2026-11-09 07:52", log)
r2 <- request_access("radiologist", "report_text", "2026-11-09 07:53", r1$log)
r3 <- request_access("unknown_account", "image_pixels", "2026-11-09 07:54", r2$log)
r3$log
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>               time request_id            role     resource decision
#> 1 2026-11-09 07:52      R0001  vendor_support  report_text  refused
#> 2 2026-11-09 07:53      R0002     radiologist  report_text  granted
#> 3 2026-11-09 07:54      R0003 unknown_account image_pixels  refused
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(!r1$granted,                                  # expected: refused
          r2$granted,                                   # expected: granted
          !r3$granted,                                  # unknown accounts are refused
          identical(names(r3$log), allowed_log_fields), # the log holds no content fields
          sum(r3$log$decision == "refused") == 2)
```
:::


**Test 2 – a wrong model version is detected before it is used.** The "model file" is a short text with the
coefficients of a synthetic logistic model. The release record holds its SHA-256 checksum.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(digest)
# A model file as plain text: identical bytes on every computer, so the checksum is reproducible
model_text <- function(coef) paste(sprintf("%s=%.4f", names(coef), coef), collapse = "\n")
sha256 <- function(x) digest(x, algo = "sha256", serialize = FALSE)

approved_coef  <- c(intercept = -2.2, cortical_line = 3.1, soft_tissue_sign = 0.8)
approved_file  <- model_text(approved_coef)
release_record <- data.frame(version = "1.2.0", sha256 = sha256(approved_file))

# On Sunday a different file was installed: one coefficient differs
installed_file <- model_text(replace(approved_coef, "cortical_line", 2.6))

load_model <- function(file, record) {
  if (sha256(file) != record$sha256) stop("refused: checksum does not match release ", record$version)
  vals <- as.numeric(sub(".*=", "", strsplit(file, "\n")[[1]]))
  setNames(vals, sub("=.*", "", strsplit(file, "\n")[[1]]))
}

data.frame(file = c("approved", "installed"),
           sha256_first_16 = substr(c(sha256(approved_file), sha256(installed_file)), 1, 16),
           matches_release = c(sha256(approved_file), sha256(installed_file)) == release_record$sha256)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>        file  sha256_first_16 matches_release
#> 1  approved f70d17b16faca3e3            TRUE
#> 2 installed 3ac397ad14f726b2           FALSE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
outcome <- tryCatch(load_model(installed_file, release_record), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
outcome
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "refused: checksum does not match release 1.2.0"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(sha256(approved_file) == release_record$sha256,
          sha256(installed_file) != release_record$sha256,
          identical(outcome, "refused: checksum does not match release 1.2.0"))
```
:::


The same test runs at three moments: when a release is received, before the server loads a model, and on a schedule
while it runs. In the case, the scheduled check found the deviation.

**Limited, tamper-evident logging.** Each event entry stores the hash of the previous entry.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
add_event <- function(chain, time, event, model_sha) {
  prev <- if (nrow(chain) == 0) "start" else chain$hash[nrow(chain)]
  hash <- sha256(paste(time, event, model_sha, prev, sep = "|"))
  rbind(chain, data.frame(time = time, event = event, model_sha = model_sha, prev = prev, hash = hash))
}
# Returns the first entry whose stored hash or link does not match; 0 = chain intact
verify_chain <- function(chain) {
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(chain))) {
    prev <- if (i == 1) "start" else chain$hash[i - 1]
    expected <- sha256(paste(chain$time[i], chain$event[i], chain$model_sha[i], prev, sep = "|"))
    if (chain$prev[i] != prev || chain$hash[i] != expected) return(i)
  }
  0L
}
chain <- data.frame(time = character(), event = character(), model_sha = character(), prev = character(),
                    hash = character())
chain <- add_event(chain, "2026-11-08 21:14", "alert_shown", sha256(installed_file))
chain <- add_event(chain, "2026-11-08 21:40", "no_alert", sha256(installed_file))
chain <- add_event(chain, "2026-11-09 07:50", "release_check_failed", sha256(installed_file))
transform(chain[, c("time", "event")], model_sha = substr(chain$model_sha, 1, 12), hash = substr(chain$hash, 1, 12))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>               time                event    model_sha         hash
#> 1 2026-11-08 21:14          alert_shown 3ac397ad14f7 c0d150a49085
#> 2 2026-11-08 21:40             no_alert 3ac397ad14f7 0bf1005f7f06
#> 3 2026-11-09 07:50 release_check_failed 3ac397ad14f7 4254a19cddab
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
tampered <- chain
tampered$event[2] <- "alert_shown"            # someone edits the second entry afterwards
c(original = verify_chain(chain), tampered = verify_chain(tampered))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> original tampered 
#>        0        2
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(verify_chain(chain) == 0, verify_chain(tampered) == 2,
          !any(c("report_text", "patient_name", "accession_number") %in% names(chain)))
```
:::


**Test 3 – recovery from a verified copy, checked with synthetic cases.** Three nightly backups exist. The newest was
made after the wrong file was installed. The restore takes the newest copy whose checksum matches the release record
and then runs two synthetic test cases whose expected probabilities were written down at release.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
backups <- data.frame(
  taken  = c("2026-11-09 02:00", "2026-11-08 02:00", "2026-11-07 02:00"),
  file   = c(installed_file, approved_file, approved_file)
)
restore <- function(backups, record) {
  ok <- vapply(backups$file, sha256, character(1)) == record$sha256
  if (!any(ok)) return(NULL)                    # no verified copy: stay on the fallback pathway
  list(taken = backups$taken[which(ok)[1]], file = backups$file[which(ok)[1]])
}
restored <- restore(backups, release_record)
restored$taken
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "2026-11-08 02:00"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Synthetic test cases with expected outputs fixed at release (probability of fracture)
test_cases <- data.frame(case = c("T1", "T2", "T3"), cortical_line = c(1, 1, 0), soft_tissue_sign = c(1, 0, 0),
                         expected = c(0.8455, 0.7109, 0.0998))
predict_case <- function(coef, cases) {
  plogis(coef[["intercept"]] + coef[["cortical_line"]] * cases$cortical_line +
           coef[["soft_tissue_sign"]] * cases$soft_tissue_sign)
}
model <- load_model(restored$file, release_record)
test_cases$observed <- round(predict_case(model, test_cases), 4)
test_cases$pass <- abs(test_cases$observed - test_cases$expected) <= 0.0005
# For comparison: what the wrong file would have produced
wrong <- setNames(as.numeric(sub(".*=", "", strsplit(installed_file, "\n")[[1]])), names(approved_coef))
test_cases$wrong_file <- round(predict_case(wrong, test_cases), 4)
test_cases
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#>   case cortical_line soft_tissue_sign expected observed pass wrong_file
#> 1   T1             1                1   0.8455   0.8455 TRUE     0.7685
#> 2   T2             1                0   0.7109   0.7109 TRUE     0.5987
#> 3   T3             0                0   0.0998   0.0998 TRUE     0.0998
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(restored$taken == "2026-11-08 02:00", all(test_cases$pass),
          any(abs(test_cases$wrong_file - test_cases$expected) > 0.0005))
```
:::


The restore skipped the newest backup and used the copy from Sunday 02:00. The synthetic cases pass within the
tolerance. The last column shows why both checks are needed: with the wrong file, all three cases would have produced
the same alert decisions at a threshold of 0.5, and only the probabilities reveal the difference. A test on the alert decision alone
would have passed a wrong model.

**Recovery test protocol (expected result).** The lab is the core of a protocol that can be rehearsed every quarter
without patient data:

| Step | Action | Expected result | Responsible |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Switch the alert off; confirm that all radiographs reach the regular reporting worklist | No examination without a reporting task | Radiology lead |
| 2 | Block remote support access; secure logs and the installed file unchanged | Access refused; copies with checksums stored | IT security |
| 3 | Verify backups against the release record, newest first | First matching copy identified; non-matching copies kept as evidence | Clinical IT |
| 4 | Restore and run the synthetic test cases | All cases within tolerance | Clinical IT |
| 5 | Re-enable the alert | Signed by the system owner after steps 1–4 | System owner |

: Recovery test protocol for the second-look service. Fictional roles; uses only synthetic test cases. {#tbl-b24-protocol}

## Counter-check {#sec-b24-countercheck}

Change one assumption and predict the outcome first. *Version 1:* the hospital keeps only one backup, the newest.
*Version 2:* to help with debugging, the provider asks for the full request, including the report text, to be written
to the event log.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Version 1: only the newest backup, taken after the wrong file was installed
only_newest <- restore(backups[1, ], release_record)
is.null(only_newest)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] TRUE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# Version 2: a log schema with a content field
debug_log <- cbind(r3$log, report_text = "<synthetic report text>")
forbidden <- setdiff(names(debug_log), allowed_log_fields)
forbidden
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
#> [1] "report_text"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
stopifnot(is.null(only_newest), identical(forbidden, "report_text"))
```
:::


In version 1 the restore finds no verified copy and returns nothing. That is the correct behaviour: the service stays
off and reporting continues on the regular pathway until a verified release is obtained again from the provider. A
procedure that restored the newest backup without a checksum would have reinstalled the wrong model and reported
success. In version 2 the schema check fails before any entry is written. Debugging with real report text is a request
for patient data and belongs in the data-protection review (@sec-b23), not in a log setting.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b24-consequences}

**A failed control test changes the plan.** The version check failed and, in the counter-check, a single-backup
strategy would have failed as well. @tbl-b24-plan shows the resulting changes.

| Element | Plan before the incident | Plan after the incident |
|---|---|---|
| Re-enabling the alert | When the provider says it is fixed | After a verified restore, passing synthetic test cases and the system owner's signature |
| Remote support | Permanent access | Access for a named ticket and a fixed time window; no read access to report text |
| Logging | Debug level in production | Event schema without content fields; schema checked at every release; hash-chained entries |
| Backups | Newest copy overwrites older ones | Several dated copies, each with a checksum; at least one copy that cannot be overwritten from the server |
| Version check | At installation | At installation, before loading and every hour |
| Rehearsal | None | Quarterly recovery test with the protocol of @tbl-b24-protocol |

: Deployment plan for the second-look service before and after the incident. Fictional plan. {#tbl-b24-plan}

**For patients**, switching the alert off costs a second look but no report, because the regular pathway never depended
on the tool. That is the design requirement behind every fallback: the tool may add safety, but its absence must not
remove any. **Ethics** (@sec-b21): patients whose report text was exposed need an explanation and a contact person.
**Regulation** (@sec-b22): a wrong version of a medical device in use is a question for the person responsible for
device safety and possibly for vigilance reporting. **Data protection** (@sec-b23): the support log is a possible
personal data breach with its own clock.

::: {.callout-note title="The incident from the security perspective"}
How is the data leak contained, how is the integrity of the model checked, and how does reporting continue during the
outage? Contain: block the access path, stop the debug logging, and ask the provider to secure and then delete the
affected log. Preserve: keep copies of the logs and of the wrong model file with their checksums, so that the
analysis is possible later. Continue: regular reporting without the alert. Recover: restore the approved version from
a verified copy and test it with known synthetic cases before re-enabling. The technical restart ends with the system
owner's signature; the data-protection assessment ends with a documented decision on notification and communication
(@sec-b23). The two have different triggers, owners and end points, and a good handover names both and the person who
decides on further clinical use.
:::

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b24-lookup}

**Reviewer question.** Which exact model version produced the results in the paper, and how could a reader verify it?
A version number without a checksum or release record, or code without the trained model's fingerprint, does not
allow an independent check
([Methods in R: Writing a report – reproducibility](https://cttir.github.io/methods-in-r/sec-appendices-d-writing-a-report.html#sec-appendices-d-writing-a-report-reproducibility)).

**Self-test.** A research group keeps its trained model as `model_final.rds` on a shared drive. A colleague retrains
the model with corrected labels and saves it under the same name. Three months later the group cannot reproduce the
numbers in its submitted manuscript. Which two controls from this chapter would have detected the problem, and which
test would you run from now on?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
First, a release record: every model used for reported results gets a version and a SHA-256 checksum stored with the
manuscript's analysis code. Before any analysis, the script recomputes the checksum of the file it loads and stops if
it differs – exactly test 2 of the lab. Second, dated backups with checksums instead of overwriting: the original model
would still exist and could be identified as the one matching the record (test 3). The test to run from now on is a
short script that loads each released model, checks its checksum and reproduces one known number (for example the
predicted probability for a synthetic test case) within a stated tolerance. Overwriting a file under the same name is
not a security attack, but for integrity it has the same effect.
:::
